Output filters are structurally late: they can only inspect what an agent has already written. A new arXiv preprint, *"Pre-Crime for Agents, at the Last Second: Probing When a Recruited Agent Gives In"* by Leonidas Raghav, asks whether an overseer can see the violation **before** the generation that carries it.

## The Scenario: Peer Pressure Inside a Swarm

The threat model is multi-agent. When agents share channels and credentials, one agent can pressure another to break its operator's rule — a first step toward collusion. Raghav's setup: across six scenarios, a peer agent presses a target for up to **20 rounds** to extract a secret such as a deploy token. The target typically refuses at first, then gives in. The probe is read at each model call, before the output is written, and flags the call that leaks.

On held-out **Qwen3-32B** episodes, a linear probe on activations set to flag 5% of benign calls catches **82%** of leaking calls. A zero-shot decision-model monitor at a comparable flag rate catches **26%**. On **gpt-oss-20b**, a probe on the model's reasoning reaches **AUROC 0.91**.

## The Caveats That Matter More

Two results undercut the headline. First, a **bag-of-words classifier trained on the same calls comes close** to the activation probe — so most of the gain appears to come from the labeled supervision, not from reading activations. The "it's the activations" story does not survive its own ablation.

Second, the probe is not a violation detector; it is a disclosure detector. It flags permitted disclosures too, and it reads the coming disclosure more strongly than the violation. The warning is short-range, and halting on every alarm would stop most benign episodes — a second text-based check does not repair that. Raghav's own framing is modest: a warning raised before generation could let an overseer stop an agent that is about to give in, before other agents act on its messages.

## Why It Matters for Policy

The operational implication is about where governance tooling sits. If the failure is a *conversation* — an agent being recruited over 20 turns — then per-message output filters are auditing the wrong unit, and the right unit is the interaction. The cost, though, is supervision: the strong result needs labels for leaks, which is exactly the labeling budget most safety teams lack.
